data.title: Zoox Begins Robotaxi Testing in Houston
data.description:
Many people just think about Waymo and Tesla when they think about the robotaxi race or competition in the United States. However, there’s also Zoox, and it has been doing a lot this year. It’s been growing its user base faster than anyone, it’s launched a new robotaxi model, it was the first to get approval for paid robotaxi service without human controls, and it began paid robotaxi service last month (after years of unpaid service while it waited for regulatory approval).

Now, we also have news the company is about to start robotaxi testing in Houston, Texas. The testing is supposed to begin later this month. However, rather than using its own clearly unique and identifiable vehicles, Zoox will initially be testing with SUVs that it retrofits and with human safety drivers on board.

The company also already has plans for a charging and maintenance depot in Space City.

“Houston is our most sprawling market to date,” Zoox noted in its announcement about this new city entry. The company added that Houston has “complex service-road networks, unique merging scenarios,” and extreme weather (high heat, heavy rain, and even flooding). This makes it a bigger challenge than where Zoox has been operating so far.

Speaking of that, Zoox is already in 11 other markets, including Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, San Francisco Bay Area, San Diego, Seattle, and Washington, DC.

data.title: US Lobby’s $1.1 Trillion Freight Rail Electrification Study Intentionally Asked The Wrong Question
data.description:
Direct electric freight rail is not speculative technology. It already operates across enormous railway systems, moves very heavy freight and works in difficult climates. The interesting North American question is therefore not whether electric freight rail can work, but where catenary should go first, where batteries or dual-mode locomotives make sense, and whether each successive investment saves enough diesel, maintenance and emissions to justify itself.

That is not the question the Association of American Railroads chose to commission. AAR had already publicly positioned itself against prescriptive rail electrification before it hired HDR to assess catenary across roughly 105,000 to 139,000 track-miles of the Class I network. The resulting HDR catenary study produced conceptual capital estimates of $870 billion to $1.1 trillion, including contingency. AAR then announced that an “independent analysis” had confirmed catenary was infeasible. There is an awkward detail in that framing: HDR’s underlying report says the system is technically feasible.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing follows how that enormous scenario was constructed, what a decision-grade counterfactual would have to test, and how a commissioned engineering estimate turned into a much broader feasibility verdict.

There is substantial useful engineering in the HDR report. Electrification requires poles, foundations, traction substations, grid connections, signal work, bridge and tunnel treatments, and careful construction beside an operating railroad. None of those costs should be waved away. But estimating the cost of transforming most of a continental railway is a different analytical task from finding the economic frontier of electrification. A multi-decade infrastructure transition normally proceeds through successive investments: rank corridors, identify the highest-value early projects, learn from them and continue while the next project clears the hurdle. HDR’s scenarios begin much closer to the far end of that process.

The international reference class also weakens the easy physical objections. India has electrified 99.6% of its broad-gauge railway, while China operates another enormous, heavily electrified network. HDR itself acknowledges electric freight operation in several countries and cites a South African electrically hauled test train far heavier than the representative North American train in its model. These systems are not American cost templates; ownership, labour, financing and traffic mixes differ. But they make continental scale, difficult operating conditions and heavy trains poor explanations for why North American freight remains overwhelmingly diesel.

The institutional context deserves attention as well. HDR is a major freight-rail consultancy deeply involved in the industry ecosystem whose principal advocacy organization commissioned the work. That does not invalidate the engineering, nor does it demonstrate that HDR was instructed to manufacture a conclusion. It does make “independent analysis” a more complicated description than the phrase suggests. AAR had already adopted a public position against electrification before commissioning a study built around an extremely broad catenary deployment and then promoting its resulting cost stack as a feasibility verdict.

That qualification is already being lost as the study travels. Reuters later repeated the more-than-$1.1-trillion figure while reporting on freight-rail pollution. Once the sponsor, scope and assumptions drop away, the number begins to look like a neutral finding about electric freight rail rather than the output of a particular commissioned exercise.

Meanwhile, the Federal Railroad Administration is asking a materially different question. Its CURRENT framework developed with the University of Texas evaluates traditional catenary alongside battery-electric locomotives, dual-mode equipment and staged deployment, with cost, uncertainty and risk treated as variables rather than assuming most of the network should be wired first. That is much closer to the useful policy question: where does the next increment of electrification make economic sense?

AAR’s trillion-dollar scenario may tell us something valuable about the engineering scale of wiring most of today’s Class I network. It does not establish whether the first economically attractive freight corridor exists.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis traces the study from AAR’s prior position through the scenario design and into the headline verdict, then examines what would have to be analyzed before “infeasible” became a defensible economic conclusion.

data.title: Volkswagen Superviosory Board Approves Plan To Slash Models & Reduce Workforce By 100,000
data.description:
In June, Germany’s Manager Magazin reported that Volkswagen Group CEO Oliver Blume had a plan to close four factories in Germany and eliminate 100,000 workers, both in Germany and around the world, by 2030. It said the plan would be made public at a company board meeting on July 9. The Volkswagen factories affected were said to be those in Hanover, Zwickau, and Emden, as well as the Audi factory in Neckarsulm.

July 9 came and went, and the plan did not get the approval from the board of directors that Blume expected. The vote was 12 against and only 7 in favor of Blume’s vision. As we reported at the time, “What happens now is anyone’s guess. Volkswagen is producing more cars than it can sell, a situation that cannot go on indefinitely. It has seen its annual sales fall from around 12 million vehicles to just 9 million. That is still a lot of cars and trucks, but the profit margins on them have fallen as well, putting the squeeze on investors.”

Then, on September 3, 2026, Volkswagen Group announced that the plan submitted in June had been approved unanimously by the supervisory board. Insiders have consistently described Blume as “determined” to push ahead with his restructuring plan. Following his initial setback, Handelsblatt reported that he wanted to implement the strategy “in stages now — if necessary, even against opposition from employees and the state of Lower Saxony”

The company already has plans in place to reduce its workforce by 50,000. The new plan adds another 50,000 to that number, bringing the total to 100,000. But wait, there’s more! The plan calls for eliminating half of all the models currently offered and still leaves the fate of four factories in Germany up in the air.

Focus On The Long Term

In a statement, the company said, “As the automotive industry and its markets undergo their fastest and most fundamental shift to date, it enables the Volkswagen Group to pave the way for sustainable long term success. The Future Plan 2030 sets the stage to make the Volkswagen Group and its brands stronger, more competitive and better positioned for the future. The Executive Board will now jointly drive the necessary measures, collaborating with the brands, subsidiaries and employee representatives.”

Blume told the press, “The Supervisory Board has unanimously approved the Executive Board’s Future Plan presented today. This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group. We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide. Over the coming years, we will invest a three figure billion sum to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger, and more competitive.”

A concept for a sustainable and competitive production structure is to be developed for the European plants by the end of June 2027, the press release said. “With its resolution, the Supervisory Board acknowledges that Volkswagen Group’s European capacity currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units and that a competitive future production allocation for the Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm plants cannot currently be secured on a staggered basis from 2031 to 2034. In parallel and in addition, alternative uses for these plants are being assessed.”

More than 40,000 people work at those four factories, which have a combined annual production capacity of around 750,000 vehicles. Fortunately, actions by the current US administration aimed at undermining NATO are providing new opportunities to put underutilized factories to good use for the production of military hardware. Opportunities are where you find them.

“People forget how big the car industry is,” Harald Hendrikse, a managing director at Citi Research, told the New York Times. “The chance of saving all of these jobs and all of this capacity with the defense industry is zero.”

Another possibility is using some of that excess factory space to build cars for Chinese companies.

Time To Step Up

IG Metall and the Volkswagen Group works council, who strongly opposed the original plan proposed by Blume, are holding their fire, at least for now. They stressed that this most recent decision prevented an escalation of hostilities between management and workers. At the same time, they said the management board now had to do its homework.

“The confrontational approach and communication by the management board in recent weeks were not constructive,” said IG Metall chief Christiane Benner and works council chair Daniela Cavallo in a joint statement. However, Benner and Cavallo said that the spinoff of the core brand was now off the table and that the attack on Germany’s co-determination structures had therefore been successfully fended off. They added that “no plant has been abandoned, and contrary to several media reports, no plant closure has been finalized. Instead, concrete solutions must now be developed for all sites, and we continue to see the management board as having a clear responsibility.”

For years, we here at CleanTechnica have been predicting major changes ahead for legacy automakers. There are millions of people who may want an automobile but who are not in a position to pay $48,500 for one — the average price of a new car today in the US. There are huge potential markets in India, Africa, and the Orient, but many of those people are not looking for a 3-row, seven-passenger SUV. They are more likely to prefer entry-level cars that are simple, practical, and cheap. Chinese automakers are only too happy to offer customers cars that are significantly less expensive.

A V8 Was Good Enough For My Father!

Many manufacturers, especially in the US, are sticking to big, hulking models with tried and true infernal combustion engines. They seem not to know or care that electric cars are now about a quarter of new car sales, with the percentage rising quarter by quarter. Volkswagen is making a bold move by proposing to prune its model lineup by half. There is no word on whether the models Volkswagen will choose to cut from its lineup will be powered by conventional or battery electric powertrains.

There is also no guarantee that the restructuring at Volkswagen will succeed. The latest tariffs by the US administration are making many of the models it sells in America uncompetitive. Its sales in China have gone over a cliff, and its sales of conventional cars in Europe have been trending down for the past several years. The only real bright spot for the company is that sales of its electric vehicles in Europe have been trending up.

Despite all the happy talk about restructuring, there is still a chance that mighty Volkswagen — which was once tied with Toyota for the title of #1 car company in the world — could experience a Nokia moment and cease to exist as a major car company. The turmoil in the industry is fierce and there is no guarantee that Volkswagen can weather the storm headed its way. What happens in Wolfsburg in the next few years could be a harbinger of what is waiting down the road for Ford, GM, and Stellantis as well. Just because a car company has been successful in the past is no guarantee it will continue to be successful in the future.

data.title: Is Owning A Plug-in Hybrid Like Kissing Your Sister?
data.description:
If you are thinking about buying an electric car, just do it, buy a pure battery electric car! A battery electric vehicle (BEV) is more reliable, more convenient for local driving, smoother, and better accelerating. You can drive a BEV anywhere in the US on major highways without worrying about charging. EV chargers are springing up everywhere, so even driving an EV in the boondocks is getting easier every year. It is better to buy a plug-in-hybrid than a pure gas car, but it’s a little like kissing your sister.

12.5 years ago, when I was first investigating the purchase of an electric car, for me, there were only two choices: 1) a Nissan Leaf, a normal feeling, 5-seater with smooth acceleration that was whisper quiet and had 80 miles of range, and 2) a Chevy Volt a plug-in hybrid with 40 miles of pure electric range. I still had a gas car that I could use for long-distance driving. I drove both. When I test drove the Chevy Volt, I found that it was only a 4-seater. That clinched the deal for the pure BEV. Also, I wanted to make a strong environmental statement, and a pure BEV was the way to do it. I’ve owned 3 Nissan Leafs, a 2019 Tesla Model 3, and a 2026 Tesla Model Y — all BEVs — over the last 12 years and never looked back. I will never buy a gas car again. The BEVs are great, more reliable, and more convenient for local driving, and with the Teslas, long-distance driving is simple and easy. The extra 2 hours charging per day on long trips is not a problem for my wife and me.

However, for my daughter it was a different story. This is hers:

“I bought my first electric car, a Tesla Model X, in 2018. Living near Salt Lake City, Utah, and with about 300 miles of fully electric range, the car was a great option for my outdoor lifestyle. There were and continued to be frequent Tesla Superchargers on all the main freeways south, north, and east of Salt Lake City. I could easily charge in my garage for all my around-town driving; the four-wheel drive Tesla handled very well in the snow and the X worked well to haul my bikes or skis for my outdoor activities. However, in the last few years, I started to notice the significant loss of range when carrying two mountain bikes on a rear bike rack for long-haul trips. The breaking point was a biking trip from Utah to Oregon where we had to stop and charge almost every hour, adding ~4 hours of driving to what should have been an ~8-hour trip.

“In spring of this year, I decided to move to my lake house in Northern Wisconsin where there are not many Supercharging stations, and also planned to do more long-distance road trips with my bikes. This prompted me to move to a plug-in hybrid. After reviewing models available, I chose the 2026 Toyota RAV4 PHEV because they had just bumped up the electric-only range to over 50 miles. I chose the Woodland edition model, as it comes with a built-in hitch for my bike rack, sunroof, and sporty styling. However, you can’t just drop down to your local Toyota dealer and pick one up — they are pretty few and far between. After a countrywide search, I located one in Chicago. Overall, I have been very happy with the electric-only range, which can be as high as 54 miles. I use the same 240-volt plug that I had installed for my Tesla to charge in my garage — it only takes 2-3 hours to fully charge, and I use the electric-only mode to drive around town. For long distance travel, I get over 500 miles combined gas and electric range and don’t need to stop to charge at all. I have been happy with the design of this SUV for loading my bikes and gear, it drives smoothly — the only thing I miss from the Tesla is the full auto-drive mode. The RAV4 has smart cruise control, which is OK, but the auto lane-assist is very lame. The hybrid has been a great choice for me to have electric-only use for my day to day driving but still have plenty of range for long trips.”

The 2025 plug-in hybrid version of the Toyota Prius as well as the plug-in hybrid version of the RAV4 used the “Prime” moniker. The 2026 versions of both are now just called plug-in hybrids to avoid confusion.

Below, you see my daughter’s gorgeous 2018 Tesla Model X at her house in Saint George, Utah. She sold it earlier this year for $20,000 in a private sale.

A strong argument for owning a pure BEV is the superior efficiency and reliability of the drivetrain. You have no oil changes, no emission inspection, and practically no maintenance expenses for the life of the car. A BEV has no transmission, no exhaust system, and no emissions control system, etc., etc. The simple electric motor could last a million miles, and recent data shows that the battery will likely also last over 500,000 miles (the life of the vehicle). Most braking is done by the electric motor/generator, so the brakes could last the life of the vehicle as well. With a plug-in-hybrid, you have two drivetrains, so you have a more complex drivetrain rather than a simpler one. However, if you are running pure electric for 90% of your driving with your PHEV, you have avoided 90% of the trips to the smelly gas station and can probably get away with one smelly one-hour visit to Jiffy Lube for an oil change once/year. However, as for me and my house, I will choose pure battery electric. We’ve been 100% electric since February 31, 2014 — 12 and ½ years.

A big argument against a plug-in-hybrid is that many owners never charge them. On standard US household 110V current, it takes ~10 hours to fully charge the battery and most owners don’t go to the extra installation trouble, and don’t pay the extra expense for a 240V L2 charger. In my daughter’s case, her L2 charger was already in place for her previous BEV, and she didn’t even need to buy an adaptor for her new car. She was also in the habit of plugging in every time she comes home. In her case, she does all her local driving on pure electric. In between long trips, she can go for months without buying gas. Also, with the outstanding gas efficiency of her RAV4, she can get a whole day’s driving on one fill-up on long trips.

If you find any of my articles helpful to you, please use my referral link when buying a new Tesla: https://ts.la/arthur73734 (Be sure to use it when you make your order). Tesla keeps changing the program, but here’s the latest: If you are buying a new Tesla Model 3 or Y and use my link, you will get two months of free Full Self Driving (a ~$200 value) on top of the one month that comes free with every new Model Y right now. This will get you a total of 3 months free Full Self Driving. It will be $99/month after that. For a Cybertruck, you will get $1000 off your purchase price. At this moment, Tesla is offering a year of free Supercharging with the purchase of a new Model 3 Premium or Performance

data.title: 10 Facts About The Tesla Cybercab
data.description:
The Tesla Cybercab has officially launched. What that means in the medium term is not yet clear, but there are a variety of facts we now have on our desk following the launch. Let’s roll through them.

  1. The Tesla Cybercab has been launched and is available to the public to hail as a robotaxi in part of Austin, Texas. (There are reportedly 45 Cybercabs launched in Austin at the moment.)
  2. You can hail the Cybercab via Tesla’s RoboTaxi smartphone app. Tesla says that when you get into a Cybercab, it will adjust to your seating position and AC preferences and will start playing whatever music or videos you had playing on your phone. (For those of us who have been driving Teslas, we are used to all of this except the part at the end about the car’s infotainment system playing the videos you were streaming. We’ll have to see that in action to see how it works and with which apps.)
  3. The Cybercab does not include a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors, and seats just two passengers.
  4. The Cybercab has a drag coefficient under 0.20, which is super low. You can tell from the vehicle design, including the large and smooth hubcaps, that efficiency was a key focus of the vehicle. (Note that the GM EV1, which had similar hubcaps, had a drag coefficient of 0.19 and the Tesla Model 3 has a drag coefficient of 0.22.)
  5. Tesla says the Cybercab’s electric motor is “18 percent smaller, 25 percent lighter, and more efficient than other top-performing electric vehicle drive units.” Again, efficiency and low cost have been key areas of focus.
  6. The Cybercab is powered by a 48-kWh lithium-ion battery pack that includes 4680 Tesla battery cells.
  7. The Cybercab is produced using Tesla’s “unboxed manufacturing” process, which is supposed to make the manufacturing line 50% shorter and dramatically cut costs.
  8. Instead of using conventional vehicle materials for the body panels and painting the Cybercab, Tesla uses reaction injection molding (RIM) — which is typically used to produce normal car fenders, spoilers, dashboards, and some other components — and gold-colored plastic. Again, this is reportedly about cutting costs — painting vehicles comes at a notable cost. (Why is the Cybercab gold? ‘Cause we live in ‘Murica, I guess.)
  9. The only sensors the Cybercab uses are cameras — no radar or lidar.
  10. The car’s butterfly doors open and close automatically.

We’ll see how this plays out. The launch is official, and there seem to be a few dozen Cybercabs on the road in Austin. Where the robotaxi service goes from here is anyone’s guess.

Anything else important that I missed here?

data.title: IFA Berlin Recap Part 1: Diverse Approaches To Sustainability
data.description:
IFA Berlin, which stands for “Innovation For All,” is a diverse technology show. There were numerous mobile, entertainment and AI-enabled devices, but there were also a range of clean technology products. On the first day of IFA, I saw several different paths to sustainability. Products from large companies and small startups. I will follow up on some of these in more depth in future articles, but a few products stood out on the first day of the show. Each of these on its own is just part of the solution. However, they each address environmental challenges and appeal to customers in unique ways.

Xiaomi Brings EVs to Europe

Xiaomi had one of the largest booths and some of the biggest news of the show. They will be bringing the SU7 and YU7 to Europe next year. Models on display included LiDAR sensors that will be used in their intelligent driving system, also to be activated next year, pending regulatory approval. No specific timing has been announced yet. Combined with their mobile devices and efficient appliances, the introduction provides an important link in the Xiaomi Human x Car x Home ecosystem.

The SU7, SU7 Max and SU7 Ultra were on the show floor, with a YU7 SUV outside the event. Updated a few months ago, the cars have improved specifications. Onboard tech continues to evolve, including an AI Spatial Interaction sensor that enables gesture-based controls, reducing the need to use the touchscreen. These vehicles have been discussed widely before, so I will not go into detail here. But it is big news that the popular, typically supply constrained models will be exported. The sporty models seem well suited to European tastes and make EVs not just responsible but also potentially compelling to car enthusiasts.

Lesstics Builds With Coconut Waste

Lesstics, a startup out of the Philippines with a history in plastics recycling, showed off Earth Board. This building product turns coconut husk waste into sustainable boards. This waste byproduct from the coconut industry has become a waste management challenge in many tropical areas and is frequently burned, creating pollution. Lesstics, using a proprietary technology, turns it into boards that can be used for walls, floors, ceilings, cabinets and furniture. The boards have a surface uniformity closer to particle board, but longer fibers give it strength similar to OSB. A proprietary bio-based polyurethane binder eliminates the formaldehyde found in typical plywood.

Meanwhile, the resulting boards are fire retardant, noise absorbing, insulating and water resistant. And it is less expensive than traditional building alternatives. Especially in places like the Philippines, were pine trees commonly used for lumber do not grow and many trees are protected. As a result, customers can receive a better performing product at lower cost that is also better for the environment.

 

Yarbo displayed their Y series yard robots and introduced their new, more compact M series yard robots, intended for lots of a few acres. Yard care can be very carbon and pollution intensive. Multiple large machines needed for different tasks have significant carbon emissions embedded in their manufacturing. Then, the small engines that run them tend to have much higher emissions than cars. Electrification can be effective on smaller yards, but scaling up to multiple acres can be a challenge. The amount of time needed to use smaller lawnmowers and equipment would be significant, meanwhile large, electrified equipment can be costly and heavy.

However, robotics can change the equation, as time becomes less of a concern with automation. While some robotic lawnmowers are lightweight and intended for small yards as a convenience, Yarbo makes rugged machines that are designed to operate almost continuously. Rather than needing a large machine to save on labor, the small lawn robots can operate autonomously and repeatedly throughout the week. Maintaining 6 acres can be easily accomplished with reduced noise and emissions. Even the smaller M series can mow 1.5-acre areas per day and cover multiple of those areas per week, unsupervised. Automation lets a relatively small machine replace larger equipment. In addition, the system is modular to manage tasks like leaf cleanup and snow removal. The tracks work under harsh weather conditions and reduce the potential to get stuck. Meanwhile high-speed wireless charging removes concerns of can recharge the battery from 10-90% in 65 minutes, reducing downtime. Meanwhile newly available LiDAR adds a level of safety. In the process, not only does lawn maintenance become more environmentally efficient, but also more convenient.

Valentin Recycles Food Garbage From Kitchen Sinks

Many people think what goes down the drain simply goes away. However, oils can create “fatbergs” in sewers, leading to blockages. That can result in overflows that contaminate nearby water. Clogged drains are often addressed with harsh chemicals, eroding pipes and potentially creating leaks. Meanwhile, any organic waste that goes down the drain, in addition to contributing to clogs, needs to be managed by sewage treatment plants. In the treatment process, methane is produced, amplifying potential climate change impacts.

Slovenia-based startup Valentin has developed a novel approach that separates out fats and organic matter from drains in a compact unit that mounts under the kitchen sink. The organic matter is dried and can be used as fertilizer every few weeks. Exhaust air from the drying process is expelled through existing plumbing vents, eliminating odors. The oils are collected and can be disposed of in the garbage every few months. In the process, safety is improved and clogs are reduced, which is especially valuable in multi-story apartments. And there is no need to run a loud disposal or have to manually clean a strainer, improving quality of life while adding sustainability.

Jackery Takes Customer-Centric Approach To Battery Storage

Jackery, who brought me to the event, will be covered in more depth in future articles, but they impressed during the first day of IFA. Recent research from Frost & Sullivan has named Jackery “The World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand, by Volume & Revenue” and “The Most Trusted Safety‑First Solar Generator Brand.” Their customer-centric approach not only offers impressive specifications at an affordable price but also pays attention to the details that make their products more user-friendly. And they are produced in the industry’s first carbon neutral factory.

As many customers are concerned with safety, Jackery introduced the FortiShield Safety System at IFA. Jackery claims this is the “industry’s first comprehensive 7-layer security framework tailored to meet the specific operational demands of every device category.” With comprehensive safety measures, customers can feel confident using Jackery batteries in the home and on the go. The resulting increased usage of battery storage also increases the potential benefit to both the end customer and the environment.

In terms of portable battery storage, the Explorer 2000 Plus V2 increases power output while becoming 12.6% smaller and 22.1% lighter. Meanwhile, the Explore 1000 Plus reduces size by 25% and weight by 9%. For battery storage integrated into the living space, Jackery had the sleek FridgeGuard on display, which we have covered before.

Moving up in size, the modular Solar Vault 3 offers improved management capabilities for balcony solar. In addition, a partnership with SunBooster Vertical was announced, expanding potential applications using flexible solar strips that can be woven into wire fences, with the bifacial panels increasing winter output.

On the larger end of the size spectrum is the new Energycore 100kWh liquid-cooled energy storage system. This could be used to supply energy storage to large residences or applications like a farm. With 100 kW of power and a UPS-like 10ms switchover speed, supplying stable power. This could be particularly where more storage is needed than he typical whole home battery, but not up to the size of many commercial ESS units.

There was also a focus on resilience at Jackery, with the American Red Cross Explorer 2000 Plus V2 displayed ahead of its US release. The battery comes in a portable 2 kWh size with new integrated automated Storm Warning Function and Emergency Reserve Mode, providing benefits in responding to emergency situations, which have been increasing in prevalence due to climate change.

However, beyond their products, my personal highlight of the show was an in-depth discussion with Jackery founder and CEO Jack Sun. We spoke about a number of topics, including many products in development that I cannot share yet. But one of the most impressive aspects about Jackery is their approach to innovation. The focus is placed on identifying customer pain points and developing sustainable solutions to address them. Those pain points could be around energy savings, resilience, affordability or even aesthetics. The problem could be with installation cost or useability. Then Jackery focuses on total solutions to address those problems. In finding those solutions, people live better in a more sustainable way.

Which gets to a larger point. While some of us strongly dedicated to reducing emissions and protecting the environment are willing to make sacrifices and deal with complexities in the name of sustainability, many people want a more comfortable lifestyle with greater simplicity. For mass adoption, sustainable technology should address customer needs and improve their quality of life. Just as there are different paths to sustainability, there are different customer needs. By focusing on customer needs, sustainability can not just become possible but also more attractive overall.

data.title: Musk Congratulates Tesla Australia — August EV Sales Update
data.description:
In a recent post on X, Elon Musk lauded Tesla Australia in reaction to this post from Tesla Australia and New Zealand: “For the first time ever, EVs outsold ICE vehicles in Australia 🇦🇺 Model Y was the #1 vehicle & Tesla the #3 best-selling brand overall for the month of August.”

“Congrats Tesla Australia!” Musk responded.

It wasn’t just a triumph for Tesla. Over 35% of all vehicles sold in the month of August in Australia had a plug! Out of the 109,000 cars sold, 27,000 were BEVs (up 170% YOY) and 10,591 were PHEVs.

Even the mainstream media is taking notice. The following chart appeared on SBS “On the Money.”

CarExpert ran the following headline and subheading: “VFACTS August 2026: EVs outsell petrol, diesel and hybrid new vehicles in bumper month. The Tesla Model Y topped the charts in a month where electric vehicles outsold all other powertrain types for the first time, achieving record market share.”

It then added: “For context, a total of 25,824 deliveries were of petrol-powered vehicles, followed by 23,608 diesels, 18,662 hybrids.”

The Australian Broadcasting Commission (ABC) came out to our humble coffee morning and interviewed Adam Nelson, Chair of the Australian Electric Vehicle Association—Qld, and myself. They were looking for some “B” footage for a puff piece on EVs and got more information and enthusiasm than they bargained for. The journalist promised a link when the footage goes to air. I will share it when it is available.

When you look at the top ten best-selling vehicles in Australia for August 2026, 3 are Battery Electric. I remember seeing this on the Chinese reports, where the top ten vehicles and the top ten electrics merged. Seems like Australia is on the same trajectory. Can you tell that I am excited! Bear with me as we explore this further.

The top ten vehicles sold in Australia in August of all drive trains were:

  1. Tesla Model Y — 6,414
  2. Toyota RAV4 — 5,470 (some of these will be HEVs and PHEVs)
  3. Toyota HiLux — 4,833
  4. Toyota Prado — 2,475
  5. Ford Ranger — 2,440
  6. BYD Sealion 7 — 2,213
  7. Chery Tiggo 4 — 2,012
  8. GWM Haval Jolion — 1,891
  9. Zeekr 7X — 1,748
  10. Isuzu D Max — 1,708

Lurking just out of the top ten but ready to pounce were the Jaecoo J5, the BYD Shark, and the Geely EX2. What we really need are some good electric utes. Then it will be game over. “Every Chinese brand in the top 10, plus Tesla, was up YoY; every other brand, in contrast, was down.” Every other brand! In Australia, legacy auto is doing it tough. As we have asked in the past, can legacy auto survive without export markets? Read our analysis here. Time is running out. Are they dead brands walking?

According to CarExpert, over half of the Model Ys sold recently have been the Model Y Long. In July, 2,429 Model YL were delivered (outselling the standard 5-seat Model Y, which moved 2,215 units). In August 2026, there were 3,236 deliveries (again beating the standard 5-seat Model Y’s 3,178 units).

We had fun checking out the Model YL at the Tesla dealership. A few years ago, when all five of our children were still living at home, we would have been tempted. Instead, we had to make do with a Toyota Tarrago. Here are some photos of the newest version of the Model Y:

I guess I have kept you waiting long enough. Drum roll….

The top ten best selling battery electric vehicles in Australia for the month of August were:

  1. Tesla Model Y — 6,414 | year to date 31,454
  2. BYD Sealion 7 — 2,213 | 17,277
  3. Geely EX5 — 1,947 | 10,737
  4. Zeekr 7X — 1,748 | 9,172
  5. Omoda Jaecoo J5 — 1,672 | 8,910
  6. Geely EX2 — 1,279 | 1,753
  7. Tesla Model 3 — 1,271 | 4,597
  8. BYD Atto 2 — 1,122 | 7,737
  9. Kia EV5 — 612 | 4,213
  10. Kia EV3 — 515 | 3,977

No Japanese? No Europeans? Toyota came in at about number 15, with the BZ4X selling just over 400 units. I am looking forward to its full electric lineup becoming available. The Mazda 6e is off to a solid start, with 382 units sold. Even dealers seem to be surprised by the new electric Mazda from China. The best the Europeans could manage was the Volkswagen ID.4 at number 20.

In the battle of the brands, BYD is #1, but not by much, leading Tesla by only ~3,000 cars — that’s only half a shipload! Number 3 is Geely, at only one third of the numbers, followed by Zeekr and Kia.

Politicians are taking credit for the “structural change,” saying it is due to the New Vehicle Efficiency Standard. My opinion is that it is due to value-for-money Chinese vehicles, and the increasing insecurity of the petrol and diesel supply — despite the continuing bitter campaigns of misinformation in the media. Whatever the reason, it is a cause for celebration in the Australian EV community.

Every time Australia takes a step forward with EV penetration, we hear the same caveat: “There aren’t enough public fast chargers.” So bleats the FCAI. My lived experience is that the charging network is doing very well, thank you, and anyone who wants the hard data can check out Open Charge Map. See the map here or here.

A recent survey by the NSW from the NRMA (National Roads and Motorists Association) points to a bright future for electric vehicles, with only 17% of people surveyed saying that they would not consider buying an EV. The major driver towards EV ownership is no longer a concern about the environment, but cost. Electricity cost at 34¢/kWh vs a petrol cost of $2.50 a litre. The main concerns appear to be “how long will the battery last?” “Where does it go when it fails?” FUD has done its job well. More information will be needed to allay these fears.

Can we reach 40% penetration in Australia by Christmas? With record solar and battery deployment, affordable, tech-packed electric cars, the Australian motorists’ future is bright and electric.

data.title: EU CRM Centre: How to Secure Critical Minerals
data.description:
How to deliver resilient critical raw material supply chains, vital for Europe’s clean tech, with investment, partnerships and industrial policy.

The EU is heavily dependent on imports of raw materials and is failing to catch up with investments globally. At the same time, the recent energy crisis has highlighted the need to avoid new dependencies on critical raw materials. The future CRM centre, supported by robust industrial policy and building on work in Member States, must provide real financial power to deliver on raw materials projects and secure resilient, sustainable supply chains for Europe.

Despite numerous attempts and good intentions, the EU’s efforts so far to secure access to Critical Raw Materials (CRMs) and deliver progress on the ground have had mixed results. If done right, the CRM centre can change that. What is needed is a whole-of-government approach, an independent mandate and pooled financial resources, as well as the tools to be able to deploy this money effectively. Australia, Canada, Japan and the US are all doing this already. It’s time for the EU to catch-up.

This is why the CRM Centre should go a lot further than mere coordination and stockpiling. It should become the financial arm of a sustainable European mineral diplomacy, steer and support national investments, coordinate the work of development banks and export credit agencies and aggregate offtake. This requires a proper budget that should come primarily from the European Competitiveness Fund and the Global Europe Instrument.

Key recommendations

  1. The CRM Centre should bring together different EU mineral funding pots under one European CRM investment strategy. This should include dedicated funding from both the future European Competitiveness Fund and the Global Europe instrument under the EU budget, as well as support from the European Investment Bank (EIB).
  2. The Centre should have the independent mandate and financial power to invest in projects across the value chain, from mining to recycling. This should include a range of tools, namely equity, loans and price support mechanisms e.g. Contracts for Difference or offtake support. Focusing solely on stockpiling and coordination isn’t sufficient.
  3. The CRM centre should adopt a whole-of-government approach to deliver projects more quickly. This means coordinating and facilitating conversations across Member States, development finance institutions, Export Credit Agencies (ECA) and other financial institutions to provide more coherent and competitive support, and direct investments towards clean projects abroad. It should provide financial support and technical assistance to steer national project deals.
  4. The CRM Investment Hub should work as a “Minvest EU” and be able to aggregate offtake contracts. This should operate as an all-in hub that unites mining companies through to offtakers to accelerate deals and de-risk projects.
  5. The Centre should act as the EU’s financial arm to support its mineral diplomacy – securing investments within partnerships, steering national investments to identified projects. It should also work in close coordination with G7 partners.
  6. Investment in projects should promote high standards, e.g. by requiring IRMA self assessment, as well as by promoting project partnerships with EU leaders in cleaner mining, and recycling technologies.
  7. The Centre must ensure traceability of black mass and monitor leakage of critical raw materials from the EU, combined with measures to address material leakage.

Article from T&E. By Emily Ritchey, Policy Manager, Supply ChainsBrussels (EU)

data.title: Donut Lab Reveals Amazing Performance Tests
data.description:
Donut Lab revealed its solid-state battery to the world at CES 2026, to the amazement of many and to the dismay of others shocked by their achievement and performance claims. No other company has a practical fully solid-state battery in production as of this writing. Many, like Quantumscape, have tried for many years, only to find that limitations exist, like the need for extreme mechanical pressures required to maintain contact between cathode and electrode. Such measures require bulky and heavy support, obviating benefits of solid-state operation. Many have resorted to semi-solid-state as a compromise. Semi-solid-state batteries were used by NIO for battery swapping, but they ceased operation since cost and other practical factors proved unsatisfactory.

Not long after Donut Lab’s solid-state battery presentation, howls of derision and a cavalcade of insults and skepticism followed. Much of the criticism, unsurprisingly, came from established players in the battery market with vested interests in legacy batteries, companies which failed to produce a practical solid-state battery, proving Upton Sinclair’s dictum: “It is difficult to get a man to understand something, when his salary depends on him not understanding it.” Just because it is new and innovative does not mean it is real and it works, and it is prudent to request data. Some waited for data to decide, while others impatiently jumped to conclusions. In this case, in response to the many critics who said it was impossible and a scam, an unusual amount of proof beyond normal practice in the battery industry was provided. It’s not that large legacy battery makers do not provide proof. They usually provide data sheets carefully constructed to show their products in the best light for intended applications, and the boring engineering details are left in the background that show the limits. Nothing to see here, just the usual. They seldom provide such extended public proof, such as disassembly and extensive tests by independent testers.

Nail Tests

In particular with batteries, some tests are demonstrated to showcase best performance in a more dramatic way, like nail penetration tests. These are important tests and do show some of the safety attributes specific to different battery chemistries. Nail penetration and other safety tests are now standardized requirements for rechargeable batteries in China, a good development ensuring public safety and aiding battery use. Donut Lab’s battery was tested at 12V terminal voltage and then did nail penetration tests that showed absolutely no fire, smoke, or explosion and very little change in temperature, a very boring and safe result. NMC produces a more exciting display with flame and high temperatures, while LFP is less exciting and produces no fire, but some smoke. Sodium-ion batteries also produce unexciting nail tests. That set of Donut Lab tests also showed that the battery was bipolar, because the terminal voltage was above 12V and batteries with different numbers of layers showed several different voltages.

Incontrovertible Solid-State Proof

Good things are worth the wait, and Donut Lab has delivered new data. The latest tests prove the battery is solid-state and the measured gravimetric energy density is 409 Wh/kg. The volumetric energy density result is 804 Wh/l. Proof of solid-state was provided in several ways. The batteries can be made in bipolar format. That means the cells are stacked on top of each other within the package, producing a wide variety of external voltages depending on the number of cells within the package. This is impossible with a liquid electrolyte in one package. Liquid electrolytes can flow freely among all cells in the same package and ions can shuttle between multiple cells spoiling desired serial ion flow through each stacked cell. A solid-state electrolyte can stay in place between cell cathode and anode without providing a path for ions between other cells. A liquid electrolyte bipolar battery must provide separate isolated chambers for each cell electrolyte, making practical construction difficult and unwieldy. The advantage of bipolar construction is that current flows through a thin depth and over a large area, providing less resistance and requiring less electrode material than single cells constructed in a pack, increasing the ratio of active material and lowering costs. In pack construction, fewer modules are used and external conductors are reduced. The net effect is higher density at both battery and pack level, even comparing to cell-to-pack technology. In a remarkable demonstration, the cell was disassembled and showed internal construction consisted of repeated layers. There was no internal mechanical isolation between layers within the package. The layers are connected electrically by stacking. This leaves no doubt that the battery is bipolar and solid-state.

Social Media Got It Wrong

While I already recognized that liquid electrolyte NMC cells could not survive operation at 100°C undamaged, that was not enough proof for some that insisted it was an NMC cell. I debunked the notion that a cell produces a unique fingerprint by showing that other cells produced similar full charge and discharge open circuit voltages. Others have gone on to add to this. The unique fingerprint theory is wrong. It is possible to alter voltage characteristics by doping and other means. Bipolar operation brings into question whether the batteries previously tested were single cell or multiple stacked cells. Bipolar operation and disassembly show the connections create a single-stacked battery, an impossibility for a liquid electrolyte NMC battery. It cannot be assumed the previously packaged battery tested was a single cell. Despite all of this, incredibly, some have mistakenly concluded that there is no proof the battery is solid-state. They are wrong. Their conclusion that Donut Lab has no credibility is equally wrong and exposes their own credibility.

An Overlooked Matter and Story — Process

While solid-state construction and extraordinary battery performance gain headlines, process methods seem to gain little attention. I explained why the manufacturing process may be more revolutionary than solid-state operation. For those studying the field, it is no secret that printing has been a major focus for the solid-state manufacturing process. There are many studies on that. Investigations have shown that CT-coatings is the source of nano pastes used with silk screen printers. A process using nanopastes and printers may not require machinery in sealed vacuum chambers, removing toxic, flammable solvents like legacy liquid electrolyte lithium batteries do.

Donut Lab says its batteries also do not require formation. Formation is a last step in battery manufacture. Batteries undergo first full charge in this step. It forms the solid electrolyte interface (SEI) layer. Cells are warehoused in racks for up to a week, requiring large amounts of storage space. This step is the most expensive part of legacy battery manufacture. Together with the large sealed rooms and toxic vapor recovery, legacy battery manufacturing is achingly capital and operating cost intensive. Vapor recovery also requires large amounts of electricity. A 1 GWh factory can cost a billion dollars. By comparison, printed solid-state battery manufacture without expensive space-consuming formation and containment rooms is estimated to cost an order of magnitude less. Together with cheaper material costs than NMC, and easily sourced and widely available materials, printed battery manufacturing could pose a real threat to vested interests with huge sunk costs that are now in danger of becoming stranded assets. There are now several companies entertaining solid-state processing by the new printing method.

Conclusion and What is Next

From this, no conclusions can be drawn about what the cell chemistry is, but we can conclude the batteries can achieve over 400 Wh/kg and 800 Wh/l in packaged form, and are indeed solid-state, with other benefits — in all, a stunning performance result. So far, other performance claims have been verified, leaving only two important remaining performance claims unsupported, cycle life and -30°C energy retention.

The results seem anticlimactic after the rancorous critics’ responses, but there they are. It is beginning to look like critics that bet money may need to get out their checkbooks or wallets. The hoopla and pressure of social media clicks has subsided for a while. We will see whether critics own up. No doubt, some critics will persist even when shown to be wrong. The battery has proved to be solid-state, not a legacy NMC battery, and bipolar capable. Bipolar operation was not a focus early on. We are awaiting demonstrations of low temperature operation and cycle life, but now that the other claims have been proven, the battery is already remarkable. I don’t think competitors can sleep easy waiting for the final tests. There may be considerable agitation and acrimony in boardroom meetings upon hearing the latest news. I expect the industrial spies will be out in droves after this, if they are not already. It is too late to tamp down interest in this battery with disparaging rumors. Things are getting serious. There is too much proof. The test results matter. There is a real battery with astonishing performance. The ramifications of these test results deserve sober consideration.

data.title: Hyundai Motor Group Partners with Oman to Drive Green Mobility Transition under Oman Vision 2040
data.description:
• Hyundai Motor Group Signs Historic Partnership Agreements with Oman’s Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology
  • The Group Teams Up with Mwasalat to Launch Oman’s First Hydrogen City Bus in Muscat
  • Oman Oil Marketing Company and EV Charging Brand EVO Join Forces with the Group to Build 240kW Ultra-Fast EV Charger Near Muscat
  • Hyundai Kefico Formalizes EV Charging Test Cooperation with EVO Through New MOU

Hyundai Motor Group (the Group) today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Oman’s Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology (MTCIT) at the Gulf Green Mobility Forum, launching cooperation in smart city development and eco-friendly mobility. Through this agreement, the Group positions itself as a key partner in Oman’s national smart city strategy under Vision 2040. The partnership runs for an initial one-year term, subject to automatic renewal.

The same visit also saw separate agreements signed with Oman’s public transport and energy sectors, including a pilot program for Oman’s first hydrogen city bus and the deployment of an ultra-fast EV charger in Muscat.

“We are delighted to establish strategic partnerships with MTCIT today. HMG is committed to helping turn Oman’s Vision 2040 ambitions into tangible outcomes through collaboration in smart cities and future mobility.” —Hokeun Chung, Executive Vice President, Head of Future Strategy Division, Hyundai Motor Group

What Does the MTCIT Partnership Cover?

The Omani government is advancing state-led smart city development under Vision 2040, with flagship projects including Sultan Haitham City. The MOU with the Group establishes a framework for cooperation spanning smart city development and eco-friendly mobility, including electric and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles. Through this partnership, the Group positions itself as a partner in Oman’s sustainable urban transition and carbon neutrality efforts.

How Will Oman’s First Hydrogen City Bus Operate?

Oman’s national transport operator Mwasalat has signed a Pilot Agreement (PA) with the Group to deploy Oman’s first hydrogen city bus, the ELEC CITY Fuel Cell, on public transit routes in Muscat. Rather than a short-term technology demonstration, the initiative is designed as an actual passenger transportation service. The 24-seat hydrogen fuel cell bus will run as part of a pilot service from the third quarter of 2026 through the third quarter of 2027.

Where Will the New Ultra-Fast EV Charger Be Installed?

OOMCO, the energy distribution subsidiary of Oman’s national energy group OQ, and EV charging brand EVO have each signed MOUs with Hyundai Motor Group and Hyundai Kefico, respectively, to build and operate a 240kW DC ultra-fast charger at a service station in Halban, near Muscat.

What Happens After the Pilot Programs?

This cooperation between Hyundai Motor Group and its Omani partners is not intended as a one-off pilot project. Throughout the hydrogen bus pilot, Mwasalat will evaluate the vehicle’s reliability under real-world driving conditions, its operational efficiency across daily transit routes, and its environmental performance compared to conventional diesel buses. For the EV charging infrastructure, the partners will assess charging performance, user demand, and commercial feasibility to lay the groundwork for future expansion.

Based on these results, measured against pre-agreed key performance indicators (KPIs), the participating organizations will explore expanding services and formalizing procurement across Oman.
